specPoints.text: understand why entropy changes occur during: i changes of state ii dissolving of a solid ionic lattice iii reactions in which there is a change in the number of moles from reactants to products

primer.text: Entropy rises when matter or energy becomes more dispersed. Melting and boiling increase it sharply, condensing and freezing lower it; forming a gas in a reaction raises it; dissolving a solid trades lattice order for aqueous mobility. This note reads entropy signs from state symbols and works the classic endothermic examples where disorder still increases.

lessons.title: Entropy and changes of state
lessons.opening: State changes are entropy's clearest signature. Melting unlocks a lattice into mobile liquid, boiling scatters particles into gas, and the reverse changes lock order back in. The entropy sign follows the state ladder: solid below liquid below gas.
keyPoints: Whenever a substance changes state, its entropy shifts too.
Entropy increases on melting: the regular lattice becomes an irregular, mobile arrangement of particles that rotate and slide.
Entropy increases significantly on boiling, since gas particles move freely and sit far apart.
Entropy decreases on condensing and on freezing, as particles are drawn into more regular arrangements.
Raising a substance's temperature raises its entropy at every stage, as particles become more disordered.

low.restatement: Melting and boiling raise entropy, condensing and freezing lower it; the ladder runs solid, liquid, gas upward.
low.analogy: A library: books shelved (solid), stacked loosely on tables (liquid), and flung across the room (gas).
low.examPointer: Read the state symbols of any equation - the ladder gives the entropy sign instantly.

medium.restatement: Order costs nothing to lose and much to keep; each step up the state ladder trades positional information for freedom, which is the entropy gain.
medium.analogy: A marching band breaking formation: individuals gain freedom with every step from column to crowd.
medium.examPointer: Boiling earns the word 'significantly' - the gas step dwarfs the melting step.

check.stem: When a substance melts, its entropy

options.text: Increases, as the regular lattice becomes an irregular, mobile arrangement
options.explanation: Freedom of movement raises the arrangement count.

check.stem: Boiling raises entropy more sharply than melting because

options.text: Gas particles move freely and sit far apart, compared with the modest loosening of a lattice
options.explanation: The liquid-to-gas step is the biggest disorder jump.
Boiling is endothermic, and the size argument stands regardless.

options.text: Gases cannot be ordered at all
options.explanation: The point is the degree of freedom, not an absolute.

check.stem: When a gas condenses, the entropy of the substance

options.text: Decreases, as particles are drawn into a more regular arrangement

check.stem: The state ladder used to read entropy signs runs

options.text: Solid, liquid, gas in order of increasing entropy
options.explanation: Each step up grants more particle freedom.
The ladder is physical, not lexical.

check.stem: Raising the temperature of a solid below its melting point

options.text: Increases its entropy gradually as particles vibrate more widely
options.explanation: Even before melting, disorder grows with warmth.
Melting waits for the melting point.

check.stem: State the entropy direction for melting and for freezing.
check.modelAnswer: Melting increases entropy; freezing decreases it.

check.stem: State which state change produces the largest entropy increase.
check.modelAnswer: Boiling, the liquid-to-gas change, produces the significant entropy increase.

check.stem: Explain why boiling raises entropy more than melting does.
check.modelAnswer: Melting frees particles to slide within a still-crowded liquid, while boiling removes the crowding entirely: gas particles range freely and far apart, multiplying positional arrangements by far more.

check.stem: A reaction turns one mole of solid and one mole of gas into two moles of solid. Predict the entropy sign and justify from the ladder.
check.modelAnswer: The gas is lost and a solid is gained, so the change descends the ladder and the entropy change is negative.

lessons.title: Gases made and solids dissolved
lessons.opening: Two everyday changes carry reliable entropy signs. Making a gas from condensed phases raises entropy sharply, as in calcium carbonate's thermal decomposition. Dissolving a solid trades lattice order for aqueous mobility - usually a gain, though the water around each ion loses some freedom, so the balance is not automatic.
keyPoints: Thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate produces carbon dioxide gas, so the system's entropy increases.
The carbon dioxide molecule is far more disordered than the solid reactant, moving constantly.
Ethanoic acid with ammonium carbonate also forms a gas while dropping slightly in temperature, an endothermic change whose disorder still rises as solution and gas form.
Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water is endothermic (delta H = +25.7 kJ mol^-1), with disorder rising as fixed lattice ions become free to move.
For ionic solids generally, breaking lattice bonds raises disorder while making solvent bonds lowers it, so the sign is not always predictable.

low.restatement: Gas from solid or liquid: entropy up. Dissolving: lattice order lost, some water order gained - usually a net gain, sometimes not.
low.analogy: Letting birds out of a cage fills the room (gas), while making friends with the neighbours (hydration) tidies their corner a little.
low.examPointer: For dissolving, name both effects - lattice breaking and hydration ordering - before predicting.

medium.restatement: The gas step dominates because a gas multiplies positional options enormously; dissolution mixes a loss of lattice order with a gain in ionic mobility, and the ledger can land either way.
medium.analogy: Empting a wardrobe into a wardrobe-sized suitcase: most clothes gain freedom, but some must be folded tight (hydration shells).
medium.examPointer: Quote the ammonium nitrate example with its +25.7 kJ mol^-1 when illustrating endothermic dissolution.

check.stem: The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate raises entropy because

options.text: A gas, carbon dioxide, is formed from a solid reactant
options.explanation: Gas formation multiplies the arrangements sharply.
No melting occurs in this decomposition.
The sign of delta H is not the entropy reason.

check.stem: Dissolving ammonium nitrate in water is endothermic with delta H of

options.explanation: The minus sign would mean exothermic.
The temperature drop proves a nonzero value.

check.stem: When an ionic solid dissolves, the overall entropy change is hard to predict because

options.text: Lattice bonds breaking raise disorder while solvent bonds forming lower it
options.explanation: Two opposing effects decide the net sign.
Solids have low but real entropy.
Water's order only changes where ions impose it.

check.stem: Ethanoic acid reacting with ammonium carbonate is notable because

options.text: It is endothermic yet its entropy still rises, since solution and gas form from a solid
options.explanation: Disorder rises even as temperature falls.

options.text: It is exothermic and disorder falls
It proves entropy never rises endothermically

check.stem: A gas molecule carries more disorder than the solid it came from chiefly because

options.text: It moves constantly through space rather than vibrating in a fixed site
options.explanation: Freedom of position is the disorder measure.
Gases from decomposition are not colder.

check.stem: State the entropy change when calcium carbonate decomposes thermally.
check.modelAnswer: Entropy increases, because gaseous carbon dioxide forms from a solid.

check.stem: State the enthalpy change and entropy direction for ammonium nitrate dissolving in water.
check.modelAnswer: Delta H = +25.7 kJ mol^-1 (endothermic) and entropy increases as the lattice ions become mobile.

check.stem: Explain why gas formation is the strongest entropy signal in an equation.
check.modelAnswer: Gas particles occupy enormously more positional arrangements than condensed-phase particles, so any change that creates a gas from solids or liquids multiplies the arrangement count by the largest factor ordinary chemistry offers.

check.stem: An ionic solid dissolves exothermically. What can be said about the balance of lattice breaking and hydration ordering in this case?
check.modelAnswer: The hydration ordering and energy release outweigh the lattice-breaking term strongly, showing that the solvent-ordering effect can dominate; the entropy change could still be either sign, so both contributions must be weighed.

lessons.title: Two solids that go cold
lessons.opening: Barium hydroxide with ammonium chloride is the lecture-theatre classic: two ordered solids form a paste, the temperature plunges, and ammonia gas escapes. Entropy wins because the products leave the low-entropy solid state for liquid water and gaseous ammonia.
keyPoints: Mixing barium hydroxide with ammonium chloride forms a paste and the temperature drops significantly, marking an endothermic process.
The reaction forms barium chloride solution, gaseous ammonia and water from two solids.
The ammonia gas is detected by smell and turns damp red litmus paper blue.
Two solids alone have very low entropy, so a liquid or gas product raises the entropy strongly.
The entropy change depends on the physical states of the products, not just on the energy changes.

low.restatement: Two low-entropy solids yield liquid and gas: the temperature drop signals endothermy, while the state jump up the ladder pays for it.
low.analogy: Paying for a house move with the freedom of a bigger city: costly on the day, liberating afterwards.
low.examPointer: The litmus test for ammonia - damp red paper turning blue - is the standard detection line.

medium.restatement: Solids hoard order; anything that escapes into gas or liquid cashes that order in. The cold paste is enthalpy's bill, and the gas is entropy's receipt.
medium.analogy: Breaking a safe open: expensive effort (heat drawn in) rewards you with contents scattered freely (gas).
medium.examPointer: Answer template: endothermic yet feasible because delta S is strongly positive.

check.stem: The gaseous product of the two-solid reaction is detected by

options.explanation: Both are the standard ammonia tests.

check.stem: The entropy change of the two-solid reaction is positive chiefly because

options.text: Liquid and gas products form from two low-entropy solids
options.explanation: Escaping the solid state multiplies arrangements.

check.stem: The lesson of the cold-paste reaction is that feasibility depends on

options.text: The physical states of the products as well as the energy change

options.explanation: Enthalpy alone would forbid the reaction.

check.stem: In the equation for the two-solid reaction, water appears as a product with the state

options.explanation: Water forms as liquid in this change.
Water is the solvent-forming liquid here.

check.stem: State the temperature behaviour when barium hydroxide and ammonium chloride react.
check.modelAnswer: The temperature drops significantly, so the process is endothermic.

check.stem: Name the three products of the two-solid reaction.
check.modelAnswer: Barium chloride solution, ammonia gas and water.

check.stem: Explain why two reacting solids can produce a large entropy rise.
check.modelAnswer: Solids lock particles into fixed, low-arrangement positions; when the products include a gas and a liquid, the particles gain free movement and the arrangement count multiplies enormously, outweighing the solids' lost order.

check.stem: A student says the cold paste reaction should be impossible because it absorbs energy. Correct the student using entropy.
check.modelAnswer: The reaction is driven by entropy: converting two solids into ammonia gas and liquid multiplies the arrangements so strongly that the total change remains favourable despite the absorbed enthalpy.

glossary.definition: A melting, boiling, condensing or freezing change, each with a characteristic entropy direction.
The regular arrangement of particles in an ionic or atomic solid, whose order keeps entropy low.
The loss of freedom suffered by water molecules as they arrange around dissolved ions.
